description: We're a team from Trujillo, Peru: 2 statisticians and 2 computer scientists tackling Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. We'll merge 20+ years of NASA FIRMS fire data into one consistent series and build a web app with a burning-activity calendar, so emergency responders can compare current fire activity against historical patterns. Our strengths: statistical modeling, time series, data processing and web development. We speak Spanish and English.
summary:
FireSync AI is a web-based prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge.

The platform integrates NASA FIRMS satellite observations from MODIS and VIIRS into a common spatial and temporal framework. It provides interactive maps, activity calendars, daily comparisons, and exploratory sensor-agreement diagnostics.

Using authentic FIRMS datasets supplied for August 2024, we analyzed 16,836 thermal detections in a selected area of the Peruvian Amazon: 2,931 from MODIS and 13,905 from VIIRS.

Our solution emphasizes reproducibility, data provenance, and transparent scientific limitations. It offers an initial foundation for building consistent historical burning-activity calendars. Full inter-sensor calibration, multi-year anomaly analysis, and predictive capabilities remain future work.
details:
FireSync AI — Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Fire Hotspots

The Problem

NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments monitor thermal activity across the Earth, but they have different spatial resolutions, observation times, and detection characteristics. Directly combining their fire hotspot records can lead to duplicated observations, misleading comparisons, and inconsistencies in historical fire activity analysis.

Our Solution

FireSync AI is a web-based geospatial analysis platform developed to integrate, explore, and compare NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS thermal observations within a common spatial and temporal framework.

The application provides five interactive modules:

  1. Fire Activity Map: Visualizes satellite thermal detections using a common geographic framework while distinguishing MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  2. Historical Activity Calendar: Organizes observed activity by month, year, and satellite, supporting historical comparisons when sufficient data are available.
  3. Exploratory Anomaly Analysis: Provides a framework for comparing activity against previous years without generating unsupported alerts.
  4. Data and Methodology: Documents original satellite records, processing parameters, provenance, and reproducibility information.
  5. MODIS–VIIRS Validation: Evaluates spatial and temporal agreement between satellite observations.

Technical Implementation

We developed FireSync AI using Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, pyproj, Plotly, and PyDeck, with HTML and CSS for our public demonstration website.

The processing pipeline imports NASA FIRMS CSV records, validates sensor metadata, preserves acquisition timestamps, and transforms geographic coordinates into a common equal-area grid using EPSG:6933.

Observations are aggregated by grid cell and UTC day to reduce duplicate counting within the same spatial-temporal unit. A separate analysis compares observations from both sensors within configurable temporal windows.

Results Using Real NASA Data

Our initial case study focuses on an approximate region of the Peruvian Amazon between August 1 and August 31, 2024.

We processed 16,836 thermal detections, including:

  • 2,931 MODIS Terra/Aqua observations.
  • 13,905 VIIRS Suomi NPP observations.
  • 12,735 observed active grid-cell days in the combined dataset.
  • 41 paired acquisition timestamps within a ±60-minute window.

The exploratory spatial-temporal comparison produced a conditional Jaccard index of approximately 0.85%. This value measures agreement under the selected comparison method, not satellite accuracy.

Innovation and Potential Impact

Our innovation is a transparent, reproducible workflow for studying thermal activity across satellite instruments without incorrectly treating their observations as directly interchangeable.

FireSync AI can support researchers, students, environmental analysts, and organizations studying historical burning activity and satellite observation differences.

The platform distinguishes observed data from synthetic demonstrations and experimental estimates. It also preserves missing information rather than automatically interpreting missing satellite records as zero fire activity.

Scientific Limitations

The current demonstration analyzes one month of real observations. A scientifically validated long-term harmonization requires multiple years of comparable observations, satellite coverage information, cloud screening, and independent evaluation.

FireSync AI does not currently provide predictive artificial intelligence, verified fire incident counts, or operational emergency alerts.

Development Process

We used ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex as AI-assisted development tools for planning, programming, debugging, documentation, automated testing, and demonstration-video preparation. The satellite observations themselves were not generated by AI.

The project demonstrates how transparent geospatial processing can provide a foundation for more reliable historical fire-activity research using NASA Earth observation data.
